title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 132 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 618–622 (Night 132, continuing directly from nights-131), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 132 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. Tāj al-Mulūk, ʿAzīz and the old vizier move their goods into the shop the headman of the market has given them and go to the bath. The headman, smitten with the two young men, waits for them, recites lustful verses, and is coaxed back into the bath, where the two wash him; then all trade poems on the bath, hell and paradise at once. The shop opens in splendour, the townspeople crowd to it, and while the vizier withdraws to plan, Tāj al-Mulūk pines for the Lady Dunyā — until an old woman comes up to him. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَالثَّلٰثُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyatu wa-al-thalāthūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the second and the thirty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and thirty-second night,
sentences.n: The print spells thalāthūn without its long alif and marks the long vowel itself with a small alif over the lām (والثلٰثون); that mark is the print's own.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْوَزِيرَ لَمَّا أَخَذَ مَفَاتِيحَ الدُّكَّانِ وَصُحْبَتَهُ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ وَعَزِيزٌ ذَهَبُوا إِلَى الْخَانِ وَأَمَرُوا الْغِلْمَانَ أَنْ يَنْقُلُوا مَا مَعَهُمْ مِنَ الْبَضَائِعِ وَالْقُمَاشِ وَالتُّحَفِ وَكَانَ شَيْأً كَثِيرًا يُسَاوِي خَزَائِنَ مِنَ الْمَالِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-wazīra lammā akhadha mafātīḥa al-dukkāni wa-ṣuḥbatahu tāju al-mulūki wa-ʿazīzun dhahabū ilā al-khāni wa-amarū al-ghilmāna an yanqulū mā maʿahum mina al-baḍāʾiʿi wa-al-qumāshi wa-al-tuḥafi wa-kāna shayʾan kathīran yusāwī khazāʾina mina al-māli
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the vizier, when he took the keys of the shop, and in his company Tāj al-Mulūk and ʿAzīz, they went to the khan and ordered the servants that they carry what (was) with them of the wares and the cloth and the rarities; and it was a thing much, worth treasuries of wealth.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the vizier had taken the keys of the shop, he went with Tāj al-Mulūk and ʿAzīz to the inn, and they ordered the servants to carry over everything they had brought, the wares, the cloth and the rarities; and it was a great deal, worth whole treasuries.
sentences.n: wa-ṣuḥbatahu, “and in his company”: an adverbial accusative serving as predicate, with Tāj al-Mulūk and ʿAzīz as the subject of this little clause. The sentence begins with the vizier alone and then goes on in the plural (dhahabū, “they went”), as the narrator's eye widens to all three. The print spells shayʾan as شيأً, with its own tanwīn; kept.

sentences.t: فَنَقَلُوا جَمِيعَ ذَلِكَ ثُمَّ مَضَوْا إِلَى الدُّكَّانِ وَوَضَعُوا أَمْتِعَتَهُمْ فِيهَا وَبَاتُوا تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-naqalū jamīʿa dhālika thumma maḍaw ilā al-dukkāni wa-waḍaʿū amtiʿatahum fīhā wa-bātū tilka al-laylata
sentences.l: So they carried all of that; then they went to the shop and put their goods in it, and they spent-the-night that night.
sentences.i: So they carried it all across; then they went to the shop, set out their goods in it, and passed the night there.
sentences.n: fīhā, “in it”: dukkān, “shop”, is treated as feminine here.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ أَخَذَهُمَا الْوَزِيرُ وَدَخَلَ بِهِمَا الْحَمَّامَ فَاغْتَسَلُوا وَتَنَظَّفُوا وَلَبِسُوا الثِّيَابَ الْفَاخِرَةَ وَتَطَيَّبُوا وَأَخَذُوا غَايَةَ حَظِّهِمْ مِنَ الْحَمَّامِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu akhadhahumā al-wazīru wa-dakhala bihimā al-ḥammāma fa-ightasalū wa-tanaẓẓafū wa-labisū al-thiyāba al-fākhirata wa-taṭayyabū wa-akhadhū ghāyata ḥaẓẓihim mina al-ḥammāmi
sentences.l: And when the morning dawned, the vizier took the two of them and entered with them the bath; and they washed and cleaned-themselves and put-on the clothes the splendid and perfumed-themselves, and they took the utmost of their pleasure from the bath.
sentences.i: When morning came, the vizier took the two of them to the bathhouse, where they washed and cleaned themselves, put on fine clothes and perfumed themselves, and had the fullest enjoyment of the bath.
sentences.n: dakhala bi-, “to go in with, to bring in”: bi- takes along the companions. ḥaẓẓ is “share, portion” and so “enjoyment”; akhadha ḥaẓẓahu min, “to take one's fill of”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ كُلٌّ مِنَ الْغُلَامَيْنِ ذَا جَمَالٍ بَاهِرٍ فَصَارَا فِى الْحَمَّامِ عَلَى حَدِّ قَوْلِ الشَّاعِرِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna kullun mina al-ghulāmayni dhā jamālin bāhirin fa-ṣārā fī al-ḥammāmi ʿalā ḥaddi qawli al-shāʿiri
sentences.l: And each of the two youths was possessor of a beauty dazzling, so the two became, in the bath, according-to the measure of the saying of the poet:
sentences.i: Each of the two young men was of dazzling beauty, so that in the bath they were just as the poet says:
sentences.n: ʿalā ḥaddi qawli al-shāʿir, “on the line of the poet's saying”: a stock way of bringing in an apt quotation. The print writes fī with a final ى (فى); kept.

sentences.t:
بُشْرَى لِقَيِّمِهِ اِذْ لَا مَسَتْ يَدُهُ * جِسْمًا تَوَلَّدَ بَيْنَ الْمَاءِ وَالنُّورِ
مَا زَالَ يُظْهِرُ لُطْفًا مِنْ صَنَاعَتِهِ * حَتَّى جَنَى الْمِسْكَ مِنْ تِمْثَالِ كَافُورِ
sentences.tr:
bushrā li-qayyimihi idh lā masat yaduhu * jisman tawallada bayna al-māʾi wa-al-nūri
mā zāla yuẓhiru luṭfan min ṣanāʿatihi * ḥattā janā al-miska min timthāli kāfūri
sentences.l:
Good-tidings to its attendant, since his hand touched * a body born between the water and the light;
he did-not-cease showing a gentleness of his craft * until he gathered the musk from a statue of camphor.
sentences.i:
Joy to the bath's attendant, whose hand has touched * a body born between the water and the light!
He plied his craft with all the gentleness he had, * till from a camphor statue he gathered musk.
sentences.n: The verse is printed with its vowels and is given as printed. The qayyim is the bath attendant who rubs the bathers down. The print divides lāmasat, “touched”, into two words (لَا مَسَتْ); read as one. Camphor is the stock image for white skin and musk for dark: the rubbing brings dark scent, or dark grime, off a white body — the conceit is left for the reader to take as they like.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجَا مِنْهُ فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْعَرِيفُ بِدُخُولِهِمَا الْحَمَّامَ قَعَدَ فِي انْتِظَارِهِمَا
sentences.tr: thumma kharajā minhu fa-lammā samiʿa al-ʿarīfu bi-dukhūlihimā al-ḥammāma qaʿada fī intiẓārihimā
sentences.l: Then the two went-out from it. And when the headman heard of their entering the bath, he sat in waiting-for-them.
sentences.i: Then they came out of it. When the headman of the market heard that they had gone to the bath, he sat down to wait for them.
sentences.n: The print has تعد, a misprint for قعد, “he sat”, corrected here. samiʿa bi-, “to hear of”: bi- names the news.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِهِمَا قَدْ أَقْبَلَا وَهُمَا كَالْغَزَالَيْنِ وَقَدِ احْمَرَّتْ خُدُودُهُمَا وَاسْوَدَّتْ عُيُونُهُمَا وَلَمَعَتْ وُجُوهُهُمَا فَصَارَا كَأَنَّهُمَا قَمَرَانِ زَاهِيَانِ أَوْ غُصْنَانِ مُثْمِرَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bihimā qad aqbalā wa-humā ka-al-ghazālayni wa-qadi iḥmarrat khudūduhumā wa-iswaddat ʿuyūnuhumā wa-lamaʿat wujūhuhumā fa-ṣārā ka-annahumā qamarāni zāhiyāni aw ghuṣnāni muthmirāni
sentences.l: And behold, the two had come-forward, and they (were) like the two gazelles; and their cheeks had reddened and their eyes had blackened and their faces had shone, so they became as-if they (were) two moons radiant or two branches fruit-bearing.
sentences.i: And there they came, like a pair of gazelles, their cheeks flushed red, their eyes dark and their faces shining, as though they were two radiant moons or two branches heavy with fruit.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bihimā, “and behold, the two of them”: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears. ka-, “like”, in ka-al-ghazālayni. The last words rhyme in pairs, zāhiyān / muthmirān: two moons, two fruiting branches.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهُمَا قَامَ عَلَى حَيْلِهِ وَقَالَ يَا أَوْلَادِي حَمَّامُكُمْ نَعِيمٌ دَائِمٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhumā qāma ʿalā ḥaylihi wa-qāla yā awlādī ḥammāmukum naʿīmun dāʾimun
sentences.l: And when he saw the two, he stood on his strength and said: O my sons, your bath (be) a bliss lasting!
sentences.i: When he saw them he sprang to his feet and said, “My sons, may your bath be lasting bliss!”
sentences.n: qāma ʿalā ḥaylihi, “he got up on his strength”: a colloquial phrase for rising briskly. ḥammāmukum naʿīm, “(may) your bath (be) bliss”: the customary greeting to someone just out of the bath. yā awlādī, “my sons”, is the older man's friendly address; the plural is used for the two.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ بِأَعْذَبِ كَلَامٍ أَنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكَ يَا وَالِدِي لَايْشِ مَا حَضَرْتَ عِنْدَنَا وَاسْتَحْمَيْتَ مَعَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu tāju al-mulūki bi-aʿdhabi kalāmin anʿama allāhu ʿalayka yā wālidī lāysh mā ḥaḍarta ʿindanā wa-istaḥmayta maʿanā
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk said to him, with the sweetest of speech: (May) God bestow-favour upon you, O my father! Why did you not come to us and bathe with us?
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk answered him in the sweetest words, “God be gracious to you, father! Why did you not join us and bathe with us?”
sentences.n: bi-aʿdhabi kalāmin, “with the sweetest speech”: bi- marks the manner. anʿama allāhu ʿalayka, “may God favour you”: the perfect as a wish, the polite answer to the bath greeting. lāysh, “why”, is colloquial, from li-ayyi shayʾin, “for what thing”. istaḥamma, “to bathe” (form X, from the root of ḥammām), is conjugated here as if it ended in -ā: istaḥmayta for classical istaḥmamta, as in everyday speech.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَزَلَ الِاثْنَانِ عَلَى يَدِ الْعَرِيفِ وَقَبَّلَاهَا وَمَشَيَا قُدَّامَهُ حَتَّى وَصَلَا إِلَى الدُّكَّانِ حِشْمَةً وَتَعْظِيمًا لَهُ لِأَنَّهُ كَبِيرُ التُّجَّارِ وَالسُّوقِ وَتَقَدَّمَ مِنْهُ الْإِحْسَانُ فِي حَقِّهِمَا بِإِعْطَائِهِمَا الدُّكَّانَ
sentences.tr: thumma nazala al-ithnāni ʿalā yadi al-ʿarīfi wa-qabbalāhā wa-mashayā quddāmahu ḥattā waṣalā ilā al-dukkāni ḥishmatan wa-taʿẓīman lahu li-annahu kabīru al-tujjāri wa-al-sūqi wa-taqaddama minhu al-iḥsānu fī ḥaqqihimā bi-iʿṭāʾihimā al-dukkāna
sentences.l: Then the two bent-down upon the hand of the headman and kissed it, and walked before him until they reached the shop, (out of) deference and honouring to him, because he (was) the chief of the merchants and the market, and the kindness had gone-before from him in their regard, by his giving them the shop.
sentences.i: Then the two of them bent over the headman's hand and kissed it, and walked ahead of him all the way to the shop, out of deference and respect, for he was the chief of the merchants and of the market, and he had already done them a kindness in giving them the shop.
sentences.n: nazala ʿalā yadihi, “came down upon his hand”: bowed to kiss it. ḥishmatan wa-taʿẓīman, “out of deference and honour”: accusatives giving the reason. bi-iʿṭāʾihimā, “by giving the two of them”: bi- names the means of the kindness.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى أَرْدَافَهُمَا فِي ارْتِجَاجٍ زَادَ بِهِ الْوَجْدُ وَهَاجَ وَشَخَرَ وَنَخَرَ وَلَمْ يُطِقِ الصَّبْرَ فَأَحْدَقَ بِهِمَا الْعَيْنَيْنِ وَأَنْشَدَ هَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā ardāfahumā fī irtijājin zāda bihi al-wajdu wa-hāja wa-shakhara wa-nakhara wa-lam yuṭiqi al-ṣabra fa-aḥdaqa bihimā al-ʿaynayni wa-anshada hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: And when he saw their buttocks in quivering, the passion increased in him, and he was-stirred, and he snorted and snorted-through-the-nose, and could not bear the patience; so he fixed upon them the two eyes, and recited these two verses:
sentences.i: When he saw their buttocks quivering as they walked, his passion mounted and he was aroused; he snorted and wheezed and could hold himself back no longer, but fastened both eyes on them and recited these two verses:
sentences.n: The print has البيتن, a misprint for البيتين, “the two verses”, corrected here. Last night we were told the headman prefers the love of boys; this is that taste on show, and the text is frank about it. zāda bihi al-wajd, “passion increased in him”: bi- marks the one it seizes. zāda / hāja and shakhara / nakhara are rhyming pairs, the second a comic snort and grunt. aḥdaqa bihimā al-ʿaynayni, “he ringed them with his two eyes”: aḥdaqa bi- is “to surround” (bi- names what is surrounded), and the eyes stand oddly in the accusative, as if he set them round the pair.

sentences.t:
يُطَالِعُ الْقَلْبُ بَابَ الْاِخْتِصَاصِ بِهِ * وَلَيْسَ يَقْرَأُ فِيهِ مَبْحَثُ الشِّرْكَهْ
لَا غَرْوَ فِي كَوْنِهِ يَرْتَجُّ مِنْ ثِقَلٍ * فَكَمْ لِذَا الْفَلَكِ الدَّوَّارِ مِنْ حَرَكَهْ
sentences.tr:
yuṭāliʿu al-qalbu bāba al-ikhtiṣāṣi bihi * wa-laysa yaqraʾu fīhi mabḥathu al-shirkah
lā gharwa fī kawnihi yartajju min thiqalin * fa-kam li-dhā al-falaki al-dawwāri min ḥarakah
sentences.l:
The heart studies the chapter of the exclusive-claim to it, * and there does not read in it the section of the partnership.
No wonder in its being quivering from heaviness: * how many, to this sphere the revolving, (are) of motion!
sentences.i:
My heart pores over the chapter on owning it alone, * and in that book there is no section on sharing.
No wonder that it trembles under its own weight: * how many motions has this turning sphere!
sentences.n: The verse is printed with its vowels and is given as printed. The “it” of both lines is the buttock (ridf) the headman has just seen. The first line borrows the language of the law-books: bāb, “chapter”; ikhtiṣāṣ, “exclusive right”; mabḥath, “section, topic”; shirka, “partnership” — he wants it for himself alone. The second makes the round, quivering thing a revolving celestial sphere. The rhymes end in a pausal -ah (الشِّرْكَهْ, حَرَكَهْ) as printed.

sentences.t: وَأَيْضًا قَالَ
sentences.tr: wa-ayḍan qāla
sentences.l: And also he said:
sentences.i: And he said besides:

sentences.t: رَأَى اثْنَيْنِ عَيْنِي يَمْشِيَانِ عَلَى الثَّرَى * وَدَدْتُهُمَا لَوْ يَمْشِيَانِ عَلَى عَيْنِي
sentences.tr: raʾā ithnayni ʿaynī yamshiyāni ʿalā al-tharā * wadadtuhumā law yamshiyāni ʿalā ʿaynī
sentences.l: My eye saw two walking on the ground; * I wished (for) them, would-that they walked upon my eye.
sentences.i: My eye saw two who walked upon the earth; * I wished that they might walk upon my eye.
sentences.n: The verse is printed with its vowels and is given as printed. ʿalā ʿaynī, “upon my eye”, is the everyday phrase for “gladly, with all my heart”; the poet takes it literally. The print points the verb as wadadtu; the usual form is wadidtu.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَا مِنْهُ ذَلِكَ أَقْسَمَا عَلَيْهِ أَنْ يَدْخُلَ مَعَهُمَا الْحَمَّامَ ثَانِيَ مَرَّةٍ فَمَاصَدَّقَ بِذَلِكَ وَأَسْرَعَ إِلَى الْحَمَّامِ وَدَخَلَا مَعَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿā minhu dhālika aqsamā ʿalayhi an yadkhula maʿahumā al-ḥammāma thāniya marratin fa-mā ṣaddaqa bi-dhālika wa-asraʿa ilā al-ḥammāmi wa-dakhalā maʿahu
sentences.l: And when the two heard that from him, they swore upon him that he enter with them the bath a second time; and he did not believe in that, and hurried to the bath, and the two entered with him.
sentences.i: When they heard this from him, they pressed him on their oath to come into the bath with them a second time. He could hardly believe his luck; he hurried to the bath, and they went in with him.
sentences.n: The print has اتسما, a misprint for اقسما, “they swore”, corrected here. aqsama ʿalayhi an, “to adjure someone to”: to press him by an oath. fa-mā ṣaddaqa bi-dhālika, “and he did not believe in that”, is a colloquial way of saying someone jumped at a chance he could not believe he had been given; the print runs fa-mā ṣaddaqa together (فماصدق).

sentences.t: وَالْوَزِيرُ لَمْ يَكُنْ خَرَجَ مِنَ الْحَمَّامِ فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ بِهِ خَرَجَ وَتَلَقَّاهُ مِنْ وَسَطِ الْحَمَّامِ وَعَزَمَ عَلَيْهِ فَامْتَنَعَ
sentences.tr: wa-al-wazīru lam yakun kharaja mina al-ḥammāmi fa-lammā samiʿa bihi kharaja wa-talaqqāhu min wasaṭi al-ḥammāmi wa-ʿazama ʿalayhi fa-imtanaʿa
sentences.l: And the vizier had not come-out from the bath; and when he heard of him, he came out and met him from the middle of the bath and pressed (an invitation) upon him, but he refused.
sentences.i: The vizier had not yet left the bath. When he heard that the headman had come, he came out, met him in the middle of the bathhouse and pressed him to join him, but the headman declined.
sentences.n: lam yakun kharaja, “he had not gone out”: lam yakun with a perfect gives a pluperfect. ʿazama ʿalayhi, “to press an invitation on someone”, a common Middle Arabic sense; the refusal is the politeness expected in return.

sentences.t: فَمَسَكَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ يَدَةُ مِنْ نَاحِيَةٍ وَعَزِيزٌ يَدَةُ الْأُخْرَى مِنْ نَاحِيَةٍ وَدَخَلَا بِهِ إِلَى خَلْوَةٍ أُخْرَى فَانْقَادَ لَهُمَا ذَلِكَ الشَّيْخُ الْخَبِيثُ فَزَادَ عَلَيْهِ هَيَمَانُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-masaka tāju al-mulūki yadahu min nāḥiyatin wa-ʿazīzun yadahu al-ukhrā min nāḥiyatin wa-dakhalā bihi ilā khalwatin ukhrā fa-inqāda lahumā dhālika al-shaykhu al-khabīthu fa-zāda ʿalayhi hayamānuhu
sentences.l: So Tāj al-Mulūk took-hold-of his hand from a side, and ʿAzīz his other hand from a side, and the two went-in with him to a private-room other; and that old-man the wicked let-himself-be-led by the two, and his love-madness increased upon him.
sentences.i: So Tāj al-Mulūk took one of his hands and ʿAzīz the other, and they led him into another private room; and that wicked old man let himself be led, and his love-madness grew on him.
sentences.n: The print spells the pronoun -hu, “his”, with ة twice here (يدة, “his hand”), as it often does; kept. masaka, “to take hold of”, is the everyday form for classical amsaka bi-. dakhalā bihi, “they went in with him”: bi- takes him along. A khalwa is a private cubicle off the main hall of the bath.

sentences.t: فَحَلَفَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ أَنَّهُ لَا يَغْسِلُهُ غَيْرُةُ وَحَلَفَ عَزِيزٌ أَنْ لَا يَصُبَّ عَلَيْهِ الْمَاءَ غَيْرُهُ فَامْتَنَعَ وَهُوَ يَتَمَنَّى ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥalafa tāju al-mulūki annahu lā yaghsiluhu ghayruhu wa-ḥalafa ʿazīzun an lā yaṣubba ʿalayhi al-māʾa ghayruhu fa-imtanaʿa wa-huwa yatamannā dhālika
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk swore that none-but-he would wash him, and ʿAzīz swore that none but he would pour upon him the water; and he refused, while he was longing-for that.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk swore that no one but he would wash him, and ʿAzīz swore that no one but he would pour the water over him; and the headman made a show of refusing, though it was exactly what he longed for.
sentences.n: lā yaghsiluhu ghayruhu, “none other than he washes him”: literally “his other does not wash him”. The print spells the first ghayruhu with ة (غيرة), the second with ه; kept. wa-huwa yatamannā, “while he was longing for it”: a circumstantial clause.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ إِنَّهُمَا أَوْلَادُكَ خَلِّهِمَا يَغْسِلَانِكَ وَيُنَظِّفَانِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru innahumā awlāduka khallihimā yaghsilānika wa-yunaẓẓifānika
sentences.l: And the vizier said to him: They two (are) your sons; let them wash you and clean you.
sentences.i: The vizier said to him, “They are your sons; let them wash you and clean you.”
sentences.n: The print has وبنظفانك, a misprint for وينظفانك, “and they clean you”, corrected here. khallihimā, “let them”, the colloquial imperative of khallā, “to leave, let”, with the verb that follows unlinked. awlāduka, “your sons”, is plural for the two, as the headman's yā awlādī was.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْعَرِيفُ أَبْقَاهُمَا اللَّهُ لَكَ وَاللَّهِ لَقَدْ حَلَّتْ فِي مَدِينَتِنَا الْبَرَكَةُ وَالسَّعَادَةُ بِقُدُومِكُمْ وَمَنْ بِصُحْبَتِكُمْ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ هَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ʿarīfu abqāhumā allāhu laka wa-allāhi laqad ḥallat fī madīnatinā al-barakatu wa-al-saʿādatu bi-qudūmikum wa-man bi-ṣuḥbatikum wa-anshada yaqūlu hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: And the headman said: (May) God preserve the two for you! By God, the blessing and the happiness have alighted in our city with your coming, and (of) whoever (is) in your company. And he recited, saying these two verses:
sentences.i: The headman said, “God keep them for you! By God, blessing and good fortune have come to our city with your arrival and that of your company.” And he recited these two verses:
sentences.n: abqāhumā allāhu laka, “may God keep them for you”: the perfect as a wish. bi-qudūmikum, “with your coming”: bi- marks the cause. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”: the second verb only introduces the quotation.

sentences.t:
اَقْبَلْتَ فَاخْضَرَّتْ لَدَيْنَا الرُّبَى * وَقَدْ زَهَتْ بِالزَّهْرِ الْمُجْتَلِيْ
وَنَادَتِ الْاَرْضُ وَمَنْ فَوْقَهَا * اَهْلاً وَسَهْلاً بِكَ مِنْ مُقْبِلِ
sentences.tr:
aqbalta fa-ikhḍarrat ladaynā al-rubā * wa-qad zahat bi-al-zahri al-mujtalī
wa-nādati al-arḍu wa-man fawqahā * ahlan wa-sahlan bika min muqbili
sentences.l:
You came-forward, and the hills turned-green with us, * and they had bloomed with the flowers the displayed;
and the earth called, and whoever (is) above it: * Welcome and easy-ground to you, of (one) arriving!
sentences.i:
You came, and all the hills around us turned green * and blossomed with flowers on full display;
and the earth cried out, with all who live on it: * “Welcome, welcome, newcomer!”
sentences.n: The verse is printed with its vowels and is given as printed. ahlan wa-sahlan, “(you have come to) family and level ground”, is the ordinary Arabic welcome. min muqbili, “of (one) arriving”: min marks the kind of person greeted.

sentences.t: فَشَكَرُوهُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ وَمَازَالَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ يَغْسِلُهُ وَعَزِيزٌ يَصُبُّ عَلَيْهِ الْمَاءَ وَهُوَ يَظُنُّ أَنَّ رُوحَهُ فِى الْجَنَّةِ حَتَّى أَتَمَّا خِدْمَتَهُ فَدَعَا لَهُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-shakarūhu ʿalā dhālika wa-mā zāla tāju al-mulūki yaghsiluhu wa-ʿazīzun yaṣubbu ʿalayhi al-māʾa wa-huwa yaẓunnu anna rūḥahu fī al-jannati ḥattā atammā khidmatahu fa-daʿā lahumā
sentences.l: So they thanked him for that; and Tāj al-Mulūk did-not-cease washing him, and ʿAzīz pouring the water over him, while he was thinking that his soul (was) in the Garden, until the two completed their service of him; then he prayed for the two.
sentences.i: They thanked him for it; and Tāj al-Mulūk went on washing him and ʿAzīz pouring the water over him, while he thought his soul was in Paradise, until they had finished attending to him. Then he called down blessings on them.
sentences.n: The print runs mā zāla together (ومازال); kept. daʿā li-, “to pray for”: li- marks those blessed (daʿā ʿalā would be a curse).

sentences.t: وَجَلَسَ جَنْبَ الْوَزِيرِ عَلَى أَنَّهُ يَتَحَدَّثُ مَعَهُ وَهُوَ يَنْظُرُ إِلَى تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ وَعَزِيزٍ
sentences.tr: wa-jalasa janba al-wazīri ʿalā annahu yataḥaddathu maʿahu wa-huwa yanẓuru ilā tāji al-mulūki wa-ʿazīzin
sentences.l: And he sat beside the vizier, on (the pretext) that he was conversing with him, while he was looking at Tāj al-Mulūk and ʿAzīz.
sentences.i: Then he sat down beside the vizier, as if to talk with him, while all the time he was looking at Tāj al-Mulūk and ʿAzīz.
sentences.n: The print has اى, a misprint for الى, “at”, corrected here. ʿalā annahu, “on the footing that”: a pretence.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ أَتَوْا لَهُمُ الْغِلْمَانُ بِالْمَنَاشِفِ فَتَنَقَّشُوا وَأَلْبَسُوا حَوَائِجَهُمْ وَخَرَجُوا مِنَ الْحَمَّامِ
sentences.tr: thumma baʿda dhālika ataw lahumu al-ghilmānu bi-al-manāshifi fa-tanaqqashū wa-albasū ḥawāʾijahum wa-kharajū mina al-ḥammāmi
sentences.l: Then after that the servants brought them the towels, and they (dried-themselves) and put-on their things and went-out from the bath.
sentences.i: After that the servants brought them towels; they dried themselves, put on their clothes and left the bath.
sentences.n: ataw lahumu al-ghilmānu, “they came to them, the servants”: the verb is plural before its plural subject, a common Middle Arabic habit. atā bi-, “to bring”: the verb takes bi- for what is brought. The print has فتنقّشوا, which would mean “they adorned themselves”; with towels in hand the sense must be fa-tanashshafū, “they dried themselves”, and the letters are probably shuffled, but the print's word is kept and the translation follows the sense. albasū is the causative “to clothe” used where labisū, “they put on”, is expected; kept. ḥawāʾij, “things, belongings”, is everyday Arabic for clothes.

sentences.t: فَأَقْبَلَ الْوَزِيرُ عَلَى الْعَرِيفِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا سَيِّدِي إِنَّ الْحَمَّامَ نَعِيمُ الدُّنْيَا
sentences.tr: fa-aqbala al-wazīru ʿalā al-ʿarīfi wa-qāla lahu yā sayyidī inna al-ḥammāma naʿīmu al-dunyā
sentences.l: And the vizier turned to the headman and said to him: O my lord, (truly) the bath (is) the bliss of the world.
sentences.i: The vizier turned to the headman and said, “Sir, the bath is the pleasure of this world.”
sentences.n: aqbala ʿalā, “to turn towards (someone)”: to address him.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْعَرِيفُ جَعَلَهُ اللَّهُ لَكَ وَلِأَوْلَادِكَ عَافِيَةً وَكَفَاهُمَا اللَّهُ شَرَّ الْعَيْنِ فَهَلْ تَحْفَظُونَ شَيْاً فِى الْحَمَّامِ مِمَّا قَالَتْهُ الْبُلَغَاءُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ʿarīfu jaʿalahu allāhu laka wa-li-awlādika ʿāfiyatan wa-kafāhumā allāhu sharra al-ʿayni fa-hal taḥfaẓūna shayʾan fī al-ḥammāmi mimmā qālathu al-bulaghāʾu
sentences.l: And the headman said: (May) God make it for you and for your sons a health, and (may) God spare the two the evil of the eye! So do you know-by-heart a thing on the bath, of what the eloquent-ones have said?
sentences.i: The headman said, “May God make it health to you and your sons, and may He keep the evil eye from them! Do you know anything by heart about the bath, from what the masters of eloquence have said?”
sentences.n: ʿāfiya, “good health”, is the usual blessing on someone fresh from the bath. sharr al-ʿayn, “the evil of the eye”: the evil eye, which praise of beauty was thought to draw down. li-, “for”, twice: for you and for your sons. The print spells shayʾan as شياً, with its own tanwīn, and writes fī with a final ى; kept.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ أَنَا أُنْشِدُ لَكَ بَيْتَيْنِ فَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla tāju al-mulūki anā unshidu laka baytayni fa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk said: I recite for you two verses. So he recited, saying:
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk said, “I will recite two verses for you,” and recited:

sentences.t:
اِنَّ عَيْشَ الْحَمَّامِ اَطْيَبُ عَيْشٍ * غَيْرَ اَنَّ الْمُقَامَ فِيْهِ قَلِيْلُ
جَنَّةٌ تُكْرَهُ الْاِقَامَةُ فِيْهَا * وَجَحِيْمٌ يَطِيْبُ فِيْهَا الدُّخُولُ
sentences.tr:
inna ʿaysha al-ḥammāmi aṭyabu ʿayshin * ghayra anna al-muqāma fīhi qalīlu
jannatun tukrahu al-iqāmatu fīhā * wa-jaḥīmun yaṭību fīhā al-dukhūlu
sentences.l:
(Truly) the life of the bath (is) the sweetest life, * except that the staying in it (is) little:
a Garden in which the abiding is disliked, * and a Hell in which the entering is pleasant.
sentences.i:
Life in the bath is the sweetest life there is, * only one cannot stay in it for long:
a paradise no one wishes to dwell in, * a hell that is a pleasure to enter.
sentences.n: The verse is printed with its vowels and is given as printed. The bath was a stock subject for paradox: its steam-heat makes it hell, its pleasure paradise, and the two hemistichs of the second line turn the usual order of things inside out.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ قَالَ عَزِيزٌ وَأَنَا كَذَلِكَ أَحْفَظُ فِى الْحَمَّامِ بَيْتَيْنِ فَقَالَ لَهُ الْعَرِيفُ أَنْشِدْ لِي إِيَّاهُمَا فَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha tāju al-mulūki min shiʿrihi qāla ʿazīzun wa-anā ka-dhālika aḥfaẓu fī al-ḥammāmi baytayni fa-qāla lahu al-ʿarīfu anshid lī iyyāhumā fa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: And when Tāj al-Mulūk finished from his poetry, ʿAzīz said: And I likewise know-by-heart, on the bath, two verses. So the headman said to him: Recite to me them-two. So he recited, saying:
sentences.i: When Tāj al-Mulūk had finished his verses, ʿAzīz said, “I too know two verses about the bath.” The headman said to him, “Recite them for me,” and he recited:
sentences.n: ka-dhālika, “likewise”: ka-, “like”, + dhālika, “that”. anshid lī iyyāhumā, “recite them to me”: iyyā- carries the object pronoun when it cannot attach to the verb.

sentences.t:
وَبَيْتٍ لَهُ مِنْ جَلْمَدِ الصَّخْرِ اَزْهَارُ * اَنِيْقٍ اِذَا مَا اَضْرَمَتْ حَوْلَهُ النَّارُ
تَرَاهُ جَحِيْمًا وَهْوَ فِي الْحَقِّ جَنَّةٌ * وَاَكْثَرُ مَافِيْهَا شُمُوْسٌ وَاَقْمَارُ
sentences.tr:
wa-baytin lahu min jalmadi al-ṣakhri azhāru * anīqin idhā mā aḍramat ḥawlahu al-nāru
tarāhu jaḥīman wa-hwa fī al-ḥaqqi jannatun * wa-aktharu mā fīhā shumūsun wa-aqmāru
sentences.l:
And (many) a house, to it (are), of the hard-mass of the rock, flowers, * elegant, when the fire has flamed around it:
you see it a Hell, while it (is) in truth a Garden, * and most of what (is) in it (are) suns and moons.
sentences.i:
Many a house has flowers made of solid stone, * and is lovely when the fire is lit around it:
you would take it for hell, but in truth it is paradise, * and most of those within are suns and moons.
sentences.n: The verse is printed with its vowels and is given as printed. wa-baytin, “and many a house”: wa- with a genitive noun, the poets' way of opening on “many a …”. The stone flowers are the patterned marble of the bath; the fire is the furnace under it; the suns and moons are the beautiful bathers.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ عَزِيزٌ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ أَعْجَبَ الْعَرِيفَ مَاقَالَهُ وَيَنْظُرُ فِي صَبَاحَتِهِمَا وَفَصَاحَتِهِمَا وَقَالَ لَهُمَا وَاللَّهِ لَقَدْ حُزْتُمَا الْفَصَاحَةَ وَالْمَلَاحَةَ فَاسْمَعَا أَنْتُمَا مِنِّى
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha ʿazīzun min shiʿrihi aʿjaba al-ʿarīfa mā qālahu wa-yanẓuru fī ṣabāḥatihimā wa-faṣāḥatihimā wa-qāla lahumā wa-allāhi laqad ḥuztumā al-faṣāḥata wa-al-malāḥata fa-ismaʿā antumā minnī
sentences.l: And when ʿAzīz finished from his poetry, what he had said pleased the headman, and he looks at their comeliness and their eloquence, and he said to the two: By God, you two have gained the eloquence and the beauty; so hear, you two, from me.
sentences.i: When ʿAzīz had finished, the headman was delighted with what he had said, and gazed at the two of them, as handsome as they were eloquent, and said to them, “By God, you have won both eloquence and beauty! Now you two listen to me.”
sentences.n: aʿjaba al-ʿarīfa mā qālahu, “what he had said pleased the headman”: the thing that pleases is the subject; the print runs mā qālahu together (ماقاله). wa-yanẓuru, “and he looks”: a present slipped into the past narrative. ṣabāḥa / faṣāḥa and faṣāḥa / malāḥa are rhyming pairs. The print writes minnī with a final ى; kept.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَطْرَبَ بِالنَّغَمَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ هَذِةِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma aṭraba bi-al-naghamāti wa-anshada yaqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then he made-delight with the melodies, and recited, saying these verses:
sentences.i: Then, in a voice full of music, he recited these verses:
sentences.n: aṭraba, “to move to delight”, is used of singing; bi-al-naghamāt, “with the melodies”: bi- marks the means, so he chanted the verses tunefully. The print spells hādhihi with ة (هذة); kept.

sentences.t:
يَاحُسْنَ نَارٍ وَالنَّعِيْمُ عَذَابُهَا * تُحْيَى بِهَا الْاَرْوَاحُ وَالْاَبْدَانُ
فَاعْجَبْ لِبَيْتٍ لَايَزَالُ نَعِيْمُهُ * غَضًّا وَتُوْقَدُ تَحْتَهُ النِّيْرَانُ
عَيْشُ السُّرُوْرِ لِمَنْ اَلَمَّ بِهِ وَقَدْ * سَفَحَتْ عَلَيْهِ دُمُوْعُهَا الْغُدْرَانُ
sentences.tr:
yā ḥusna nārin wa-al-naʿīmu ʿadhābuhā * tuḥyā bihā al-arwāḥu wa-al-abdānu
fa-iʿjab li-baytin lā yazālu naʿīmuhu * ghaḍḍan wa-tūqadu taḥtahu al-nīrānu
ʿayshu al-surūri li-man alamma bihi wa-qad * safaḥat ʿalayhi dumūʿuhā al-ghudrānu
sentences.l:
O the beauty of a fire, and the bliss (is) its torment, * by which the souls and the bodies are given-life!
So marvel at a house whose bliss does-not-cease * fresh, while the fires are kindled beneath it.
The life of the joy (is) for whoever calls-at it, when * the pools have poured over him their tears.
sentences.i:
What a lovely fire, whose torment is bliss, * that gives new life to souls and bodies!
Marvel at a house whose joys stay ever fresh * while fires are kindled under it.
A life of gladness for whoever calls there, * when the pools have shed their tears upon him.
sentences.n: The verse is printed with its vowels and is given as printed. yā ḥusna, “O the beauty of”: an exclamation of wonder, run together in the print (يَاحُسْنَ), as is lā yazālu (لَايَزَالُ). The print points dumūʿuhā, “their tears”, as a nominative where the object of safaḥat would be accusative (dumūʿahā); kept. The pools are the bath's basins; their “tears” are the water poured over the bather.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَرَّحَ فِي رِيَاضِ حُسْنِهِمَا نَظَرَ الْعَيْنِ وَأَنْشَدَ هَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: thumma sarraḥa fī riyāḍi ḥusnihimā naẓara al-ʿayni wa-anshada hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: Then he let-roam in the meadows of their beauty the gaze of the eye, and recited these two verses:
sentences.i: Then he let his eyes wander through the gardens of their beauty, and recited these two verses:
sentences.n: sarraḥa, “to let out to graze”, is used of turning herds loose in pasture; here the gaze grazes in their beauty.

sentences.t:
وَافِيْتُ مَنْزِلَهُ فَلَمْ اَرَ حَاجِبًا * اِلَّا وَيَلْقَانِي بِوَجْهٍ ضَاحِكِ
وَدَخَلْتُ جَنَّتَهُ وَزُرْتُ جَحِيْمَهُ * فَشَكَرْتُ رِضْوَانًا وَرَأْفَةَ مَالِكِ
sentences.tr:
wāfītu manzilahu fa-lam ara ḥājiban * illā wa-yalqānī bi-wajhin ḍāḥiki
wa-dakhaltu jannatahu wa-zurtu jaḥīmahu * fa-shakartu riḍwānan wa-raʾfata māliki
sentences.l:
I came to his dwelling, and I saw not a doorkeeper * except (that) he meets me with a face laughing;
and I entered his Garden and visited his Hell, * and I thanked Riḍwān and the mercy of Mālik.
sentences.i:
I came to his house and found no doorkeeper * who did not greet me with a laughing face;
I entered his paradise and visited his hell, * and gave thanks to Riḍwān and to Mālik for his mercy.
sentences.n: The verse is printed with its vowels and is given as printed. Riḍwān is the angel who keeps the gate of Paradise, Mālik the angel who keeps Hell: the bath's owner is both, and the joke is that here even Mālik is kind. The name Riḍwān also means “good pleasure”, and mālik also means “owner”. ḍāḥiki, ending in -i for the rhyme, is the adjective of wajhin, “a laughing face”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعُوا ذَلِكَ تَعَجَّبُوا مِنْ هَذِةِ الْأَبْيَاتِ ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْعَرِيفَ عَزَمَ عَلَيْهِمْ فَامْتَنَعُوا وَمَضَوْا إِلَى مَنْزِلِهِمْ لِيَسْتَرِيحُوا مِنْ شِدَّةِ حَرِّ الْحَمَّامِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿū dhālika taʿajjabū min hādhihi al-abyāti thumma inna al-ʿarīfa ʿazama ʿalayhim fa-imtanaʿū wa-maḍaw ilā manzilihim li-yastarīḥū min shiddati ḥarri al-ḥammāmi
sentences.l: And when they heard that, they marvelled at these verses. Then (truly) the headman pressed (an invitation) on them, but they refused, and went to their lodging to rest from the severity of the heat of the bath.
sentences.i: When they heard this they admired the verses. Then the headman pressed them to be his guests, but they declined and went back to their lodging to rest from the fierce heat of the bath.
sentences.n: li-yastarīḥū, “so that they might rest”: li- gives the purpose. The print spells hādhihi with ة (هذة); kept.

sentences.t: فَاسْتَرَاحُوا وَأَكَلُوا وَشَرِبُوا وَبَاتُوا تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ فِي مَنْزِلِهِمْ عَلَى أَتَمِّ مَا يَكُونُ مِنَ الْحَظِّ وَالسُّرُورِ
sentences.tr: fa-istarāḥū wa-akalū wa-sharibū wa-bātū tilka al-laylata fī manzilihim ʿalā atammi mā yakūnu mina al-ḥaẓẓi wa-al-surūri
sentences.l: So they rested and ate and drank and spent-the-night that night in their lodging, upon the most-complete of what can be of the pleasure and the joy.
sentences.i: So they rested, ate and drank, and spent that night in their lodging in the greatest possible pleasure and happiness.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ قَامُوا مِنْ نَوْمِهِمْ وَتَوَضَّؤا وَصَلَّوْا فَرْضَهُمْ وَاصْطَبَحُوا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu qāmū min nawmihim wa-tawaḍḍaʾū wa-ṣallaw farḍahum wa-iṣṭabaḥū
sentences.l: And when the morning dawned, they rose from their sleep, and performed-ablution and prayed their obligatory (prayer), and took-the-morning-draught.
sentences.i: When morning came they rose from sleep, made their ablutions, said the prescribed prayer, and took their morning drink.
sentences.n: farḍ, “obligation”, here the prescribed dawn prayer. iṣṭabaḥa is “to take the morning draught”, usually of wine; it can also mean simply to breakfast. The print writes tawaḍḍaʾū with ؤ and a bare alif (توضؤا); kept.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ وَفُتِحَتِ الدَّكَاكِينُ وَالْأَسْوَاقُ قَامُوا بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ وَتَمَشَّوْا وَخَرَجُوا مِنَ الْمَنْزِلِ وَأَتَوْا إِلَى السُّوقِ وَفَتَحُوا الدُّكَّانَ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā ṭalaʿati al-shamsu wa-futiḥati al-dakākīnu wa-al-aswāqu qāmū baʿda dhālika wa-tamashshaw wa-kharajū mina al-manzili wa-ataw ilā al-sūqi wa-fataḥū al-dukkāna
sentences.l: And when the sun rose and the shops and the markets were opened, they rose after that and walked-along, and went-out from the lodging and came to the market and opened the shop.
sentences.i: When the sun had risen and the shops and markets were open, they got up, strolled out of the house, came to the market and opened the shop.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتِ الْغِلْمَانُ قَدْ هَيَّأُوهَا أَحْسَنَ هَيْئَةٍ وَفَرَشُوا فِيهَا السَّجَاجِيدَ وَالْبُسُطَ الْحَرِيرَ وَوَضَعُوا فِيهَا مَرْتَبَتَيْنِ كُلُّ مَرْتَبَةٍ تُسَاوِي مِائَةَ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: wa-kānati al-ghilmānu qad hayyaʾūhā aḥsana hayʾatin wa-farashū fīhā al-sajājīda wa-al-busuṭa al-ḥarīra wa-waḍaʿū fīhā martabatayni kullu martabatin tusāwī miʾata dīnārin
sentences.l: And the servants had prepared it the best preparation, and spread in it the carpets and the rugs the silk, and placed in it two cushion-seats, each cushion-seat worth a hundred dinars.
sentences.i: The servants had fitted it out in the finest style, spreading prayer carpets and silk rugs, and setting in it two cushioned seats, each worth a hundred dinars.
sentences.n: kānati al-ghilmānu, “the servants were”: a feminine verb, as often with a broken plural, then hayyaʾūhā in the masculine plural. The print sets the marks on هَيَّأوها itself; the rest of the pointing is ours. aḥsana hayʾatin, “the best of fittings”: an inner accusative. The sajjāda is a small carpet, often a prayer rug; the martaba a raised cushioned seat.

sentences.t: وَجَعَلُوا فَوْقَ كُلِّ مَرْتَبَةٍ نِطْعًا مُلُوكِيًّا دَائِرُهُ شَرِيطٌ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ وَفِي وَسَطِ الدُّكَّانِ الْفَرْشُ الْفَائِقُ اللَّائِقُ بِالْمَقَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-jaʿalū fawqa kulli martabatin niṭʿan mulūkiyyan dāʾiruhu sharīṭun mina al-dhahabi wa-fī wasaṭi al-dukkāni al-farshu al-fāʾiqu al-lāʾiqu bi-al-maqāmi
sentences.l: And they put above each cushion-seat a leather-cover royal, its border a band of the gold; and in the middle of the shop the furnishing, the surpassing, the befitting the station.
sentences.i: Over each seat they laid a leather cover fit for kings, edged all round with gold braid; and in the middle of the shop were furnishings of the finest, as befitted the place.
sentences.n: A niṭʿ is a spread of leather, used as a mat or seat-cover. mulūkī, “royal, kingly”, is formed from the plural mulūk. fāʾiq / lāʾiq rhyme. lāʾiq bi-, “suited to”: bi- names what it suits.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ عَلَى مَرْتَبَةٍ وَعَزِيزٌ عَلَى الْأُخْرَى وَجَلَسَ الْوَزِيرُ فِي وَسَطِ الدُّكَّانِ وَوَقَفَ الْغِلْمَانُ بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasa tāju al-mulūki ʿalā martabatin wa-ʿazīzun ʿalā al-ukhrā wa-jalasa al-wazīru fī wasaṭi al-dukkāni wa-waqafa al-ghilmānu bayna aydīhim
sentences.l: Then Tāj al-Mulūk sat on a cushion-seat and ʿAzīz on the other, and the vizier sat in the middle of the shop, and the servants stood between their hands.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk sat on one seat and ʿAzīz on the other, the vizier sat in the middle of the shop, and the servants stood before them, ready to serve.
sentences.n: bayna aydīhim, “between their hands”: in attendance before them.

sentences.t: وَتَسَامَعَتْ بِهِمْ أَهْلُ الْبَلَدِ فَازْدَحَمُوا عَلَيْهِمْ فَبَاعُوا بَعْضَ بَضَائِعِهِمْ وَبَعْضَ أَقْمِشَتِهِمْ وَشَاعَ فِى الْمَدِينَةِ ذِكْرُ تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ وَحُسْنِهِ وَجَمَالِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-tasāmaʿat bihim ahlu al-baladi fa-izdaḥamū ʿalayhim fa-bāʿū baʿḍa baḍāʾiʿihim wa-baʿḍa aqmishatihim wa-shāʿa fī al-madīnati dhikru tāji al-mulūki wa-ḥusnihi wa-jamālihi
sentences.l: And the people of the town heard-of-them-one-from-another, and crowded upon them; so they sold some of their wares and some of their cloths. And there spread in the city the mention of Tāj al-Mulūk and of his comeliness and his beauty.
sentences.i: Word of them went round among the townspeople, who came crowding to them, and they sold some of their wares and some of their cloth; and talk of Tāj al-Mulūk, of his good looks and his beauty, spread through the city.
sentences.n: tasāmaʿa bi-, “to hear of, by word passed from one to another”: bi- names what is heard of. The verb is feminine with ahl, “people”, taken as a collective.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَقَامُوا عَلَى ذَلِكَ أَيَّامًا وَفِي كُلِّ يَوْمٍ تَتَزَايَدُ النَّاسُ عَلَيْهِمْ وَتَهْرَعُ إِلَيْهِمْ
sentences.tr: thumma aqāmū ʿalā dhālika ayyāman wa-fī kulli yawmin tatazāyadu al-nāsu ʿalayhim wa-tahraʿu ilayhim
sentences.l: Then they remained upon that (for) days, and in every day the people increase upon them and hurry to them.
sentences.i: So they went on for some days, and every day more people came to them and hurried to their shop.
sentences.n: The verbs for al-nās, “the people”, are feminine, as for a collective. tahraʿu, “they hurry”, from hariʿa, “to hasten”; the passive of the causative, uhriʿa, “to be driven in haste”, is the commoner classical way of saying it.

sentences.t: فَأَقْبَلَ الْوَزِيرُ عَلَى تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ وَأَوْصَاهُ بِكِتْمَانِ سِرِّهِ وَأَوْصَى عَلَيْهِ عَزِيزًا وَمَضَى الْوَزِيرُ إِلَى الدَّارِ لِيَخْتَلِيَ بِنَفْسِهِ وَيُدَبِّرَ أَمْرًا يَعُودُ نَفْعُهُ عَلَيْهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-aqbala al-wazīru ʿalā tāji al-mulūki wa-awṣāhu bi-kitmāni sirrihi wa-awṣā ʿalayhi ʿazīzan wa-maḍā al-wazīru ilā al-dāri li-yakhtaliya bi-nafsihi wa-yudabbira amran yaʿūdu nafʿuhu ʿalayhim
sentences.l: Then the vizier turned to Tāj al-Mulūk and enjoined him to the keeping of his secret, and charged ʿAzīz over him; and the vizier went to the house so that he might be-alone with himself and contrive a matter whose benefit returns upon them.
sentences.i: Then the vizier turned to Tāj al-Mulūk and charged him to keep his secret, and put ʿAzīz in charge of him; and he went off to the house to be alone and think out a plan that would turn to their advantage.
sentences.n: awṣāhu bi-, “to enjoin on someone”: bi- names what is enjoined. awṣā ʿalayhi ʿazīzan, “charged ʿAzīz with him”: ʿalā names the one to be looked after. li-yakhtaliya, “so that he might be alone”: li- of purpose; ikhtalā bi-nafsihi, “to be alone with himself”.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ وَعَزِيزٌ يَتَحَادَثَانِ وَتَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ يَقُولُ لِعَزِيزٍ عَسَى أَحَدٌ يَجِئُ مِنْ عِنْدِ السِّتِّ دُنْيَا
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra tāju al-mulūki wa-ʿazīzun yataḥādathāni wa-tāju al-mulūki yaqūlu li-ʿazīzin ʿasā aḥadun yajīʾu min ʿindi al-sitti dunyā
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk and ʿAzīz began conversing-together, and Tāj al-Mulūk saying to ʿAzīz: Perhaps someone comes from the presence of the Lady Dunyā.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk and ʿAzīz would sit talking together, and Tāj al-Mulūk kept saying to ʿAzīz, “Perhaps someone will come from the Lady Dunyā.”
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “began to, took to”. ʿasā aḥadun yajīʾu, “perhaps someone comes”: in the classical language ʿasā takes an, here it is followed by the bare verb. al-sitt, “the lady”, is the everyday title (from sayyida). The print writes yajīʾu with ئ (يجئ); kept.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ عَلَى ذَلِكَ أَيَّامًا وَلَيَالِيَ وَهُوَ قَلِقُ الْفُؤَادِ لَا يَعْرِفُ النَّوْمَ وَلَا الرُّقَادَ وَقَدْ تَمَكَّنَ مِنْهُ الْغَرَامُ وَزَادَ بِهِ الْوَجْدُ وَالْهُيَامُ حَتَّى حُرِمَ لَذِيذَ الْمَنَامِ وَامْتَنَعَ مِنَ الشَّرَابِ وَالطَّعَامِ وَكَانَ كَالْبَدْرِ لَيْلَةَ التَّمَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal tāju al-mulūki ʿalā dhālika ayyāman wa-layāliya wa-huwa qaliqu al-fuʾādi lā yaʿrifu al-nawma wa-lā al-ruqāda wa-qad tamakkana minhu al-gharāmu wa-zāda bihi al-wajdu wa-al-huyāmu ḥattā ḥurima ladhīdha al-manāmi wa-imtanaʿa mina al-sharābi wa-al-ṭaʿāmi wa-kāna ka-al-badri laylata al-tamāmi
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk did not cease upon that, days and nights, while he (was) restless of the heart, not knowing the sleep nor the slumber; and the love-torment had taken-hold of him, and the passion and the love-madness had increased in him, until he was deprived of the sweet of the sleep and abstained from the drink and the food; and he was like the full-moon (on the) night of the completion.
sentences.i: So Tāj al-Mulūk went on, days and nights, restless at heart, knowing neither sleep nor slumber; love had mastered him, and passion and longing grew in him, until he was robbed of sweet sleep and turned away from food and drink — and yet he was like the moon on the night it is full.
sentences.n: A run of rhymed prose: ruqād, huyām, manām, ṭaʿām, tamām. zāda bihi, “increased in him”: bi- marks the one it seizes. ka-al-badri, “like the full moon”: his beauty is undimmed by his pining.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ جَالِسٌ وَإِذَا هُوَ بِامْرَأَةٍ عَجُوزٍ أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā tāju al-mulūki jālisun wa-idhā huwa bi-imraʾatin ʿajūzin aqbalat ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And while Tāj al-Mulūk (was) sitting, behold, he (was) with an old woman (who) came toward him
sentences.i: Then one day, as Tāj al-Mulūk was sitting there, an old woman came up to him —
sentences.n: wa-idhā huwa bi-, “and behold, he (found himself) with”: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
